docs.title: CSC cPouta User Guide
docs.text:
Welcome!

This guide helps new users work with CSC’s cPouta cloud environment. Use the navigation on the left to browse sections.

This documentation includes:

  • step-by-step instructions
  • screenshots
  • copy-paste-ready commands
  • troubleshooting notes
  • an optional demo website you can deploy on cPouta

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: Version: 1.0 Last updated: December 2025 Authors: Antti Huttunen & Jere Mäkivierikko Organization: OAMK – Degree Programme in Information Technology

docs.title: 1.1 Purpose of this guide
docs.text:
This guide provides beginner friendly introduction to CSC’s cPouta cloud platform. By following these steps, you will learn how to:

  • create a CSC account
  • create a project
  • generate SSH keys
  • configure security groups
  • launch a virtual machine
  • connect via SSH
  • install software
  • host a simple website

docs.title: 1.2 Who is this guide for?
docs.text:
• OAMK students
  • OAMK staff
  • Anyone unfamiliar with Linux or cloud platforms

docs.title: How to use this guide
docs.text:
• All commands are copy-paste-friendly.
  • If copy-paste breaks, paste into Notepad or a plain-text editor first.
  • Screenshots may differ slightly from the current CSC interface.
  • SSH client, used in this guide is PuTTY. Download PuTTY client from links below:
PuTTY download: http://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~sgtatham/putty/download.html PowerShell: https://docs.csc.fi/cloud/pouta/launch-vm-from-web-gui/#windows-powershell Linux and Mac: https://docs.csc.fi/cloud/pouta/launch-vm-from-web-gui/#linux-and-mac
  • Follow the chapters in order unless you know what you’re doing.

docs.title: 2.1 Create a CSC user account
docs.text:
1. Go to https://my.csc.fi
  2. Select Create account
  3. Log in using your HAKA credentials
  4. Confirm your email and set your My CSC password (this is not used to login).
  5. After your account is approved, log in again using HAKA credentials. You will now see the MyCSC dashboard, which confirms the account is active.

Note: If you get Web login service – Stale request error (picture below), close the tab and try again. It sometimes needs multiple attempts.

docs.title: 3. Creating a New Project
docs.text: You must create a CSC project before you can launch virtual machines in cPouta.

docs.title: 3.1 Create a project in MyCSC
docs.text:
1. Log in to MyCSC with your HAKA account
  2. Go to Projects → + New project
  3. Fill in the required fields and choose End date for the project
  4. Select cPouta as your service
  5. Choose a resource package
  6. Read and accept the terms of use
  7. Once created, go to Profile and + Enable CSC Multi-Factor Authentication. This is required to use cPouta. For more information: https://docs.csc.fi/accounts/mfa/
  8. The project will appear in Projects overview, and you can access the cPouta dashboard through Services → (cPouta) Login with your HAKA credentials. You can add members to your project with either + Add members or Generate invitation link.

docs.title: 3.2 Accessing the cPouta dashboard
docs.text: Once your CSC account and project are created, you can access cPouta cloud management interface by logging in with your Haka credentials. You will now see the cPouta dashboard.

docs.title: 4. Creating a Virtual Machine
docs.text:
Before launching a VM, you need to configure:

  • SSH keys
  • Security groups (firewall rules)

docs.title: 4.1 Setting up SSH keys
docs.text:
1. Go to Compute → Key Pairs
  2. Select + Create Key Pair
  3. Enter a name for the key
  4. Key Type should be SSH Key
  5. Click + Create Key Pair. This will download the key as .pem file

Important: This is your private key. It cannot be downloaded again.

Keep it secret! Keep it safe!

docs.title: 4.1.1 PuTTY – converting .pem to .ppk
docs.text:
1. Run PuTTYgen and click Load
  2. Change file filter to All files (.) and select the key you created (keyname.pem)

  3. Set a password to the key. This is not required, but it is advised. Click Save private key as .ppk

    Now we can use the key in PuTTY to connect to a Virtual Machine.

  4. Run PuTTY and load the .ppk SSH key.

  5. Go to Connection → SSH → Auth → Credentials and under Private key file for authentication, use the Browse button to select the converted .ppk file.

  6. Go to Session and under Saved Sessions write the name of the new session and click save.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Firewalls and Security Groups
docs.text: Security groups in cPouta act as firewall rule sets that control what network traffic is allowed to connect your virtual machine.

docs.title: Create a security group
docs.text:
1. Go to Network → Security Groups and click + Create Security Group. Name it and write a description.
  2. You should automatically be in Manage Rules section, if not click Manage Rules on the Security Group you just created. Click + Add rule
  3. Use the SSH rule and click Add. With CIDR you can define IP addresses allowed to connect.

docs.title: CIDR explanation
docs.text:
• /32 = only your exact IP address
  • /24 = your entire local subnet
  • 0.0.0.0/0 = open to the world (not recommended)

docs.title: 5.1 Creating a virtual machine
docs.text:
Once the SSH keys and security groups are ready, you can launch a new virtual machine.

  1. In cPouta dashboard navigate to Compute → Instances and click Launch Instance

  2. Add Instance Name and select the number of instances (Count) you wish to create. Click Next.
  3. Select your Instance Boot Source. Select “image” in the drop-down menu and click on the ↑ Click Next. In this guide we are using Ubuntu-24.04 but image source might change.

  4. Select the Flavour which means the “size” of the Virtual Machine by clicking on the ↑ icon.
  5. In Networks section, make sure your project is allocated.
  6. In Security Groups section assign the security group that was created earlier with ↑ icon.

  7. In Key Pair section make sure the Key Pair created earlier is Allocated, if not select it with ↑ icon. Important: SSH keys must be selected at this stage, they cannot be added later. If no key is chosen, delete the VM and create a new one.
  8. You can now click Launch Instance to create the Virtual Machine.

docs.title: 5.2 Assigning a Floating IP
docs.text:
To connect to your virtual machine, you must assign a Floating IP (public IP):

  1. In the cPouta dashboard, go to Compute → Instances. Here you should see the new instance.
  2. On the right side under Actions, open drop-down menu and select Associate Floating IP.

  3. Under IP Address, choose an available floating IP. If you see “No floating IP addresses allocated” click the + button and click Allocate IP.

  4. Under Port to be associated, select your virtual machine and click Associate.

  5. You can now find Floating IP of your virtual machine on the Instances page.

docs.title: 6. Connecting to Your Virtual Machine
docs.text: After assigning a Floating IP to your virtual machine, you can connect to it using SSH. In this guide we use PuTTY.

docs.title: 6.1 Connecting with PuTTY (Windows)
docs.text:
1. Open PuTTY and Load the session created earlier.
  2. In Host Name (or IP address), enter: ubuntu@(your Floating IP here) and click Open. Note: For your Floating IP check the guide 5.2 step 5. 192.168.x.xxx is your virtual machine local IP, DO NOT use this.
  3. You should now be connected to the virtual machine and see the terminal.
  4. After logging in, update the system with the script below. This ensures your VM has the latest security patches.

Run:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

docs.title: 6.2 Common connection issues
docs.text:
• Permission denied (publickey) → Wrong key file or not assigned during VM creation

    • In PuTTY go to Category → Connection → SSH → Auth → Credentials → Browse… (Private key file for authentication:) and select the correct .ppk file

  • CIDR too strict → If your IP changed (e.g., mobile hotspot, different networks etc.) rules may block you.

    • Update your SSH rule CIDR to match your new IP

docs.title: 7. Installing Docker
docs.text: If you want, you can check docker documentation for ubuntu: : https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/

docs.title: 7.1 Add Docker repositories
docs.text:
Copy bash scripts below and paste them to SSH terminal. Note you might need to paste text using SHIFT + INSERT. Press ENTER after scripts are pasted to terminal. Monitor terminal output. If prompted yes or no, write yes or y and press ENTER

Run the following:

# Add Docker's official GPG key:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

# Add the repository to Apt sources:
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources <<EOF
Types: deb
URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu
Suites: $(. /etc/os-release && echo "${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-$VERSION_CODENAME}")
Components: stable
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
EOF

sudo apt update

docs.title: 7.2 Install Docker
docs.text:
Copy bash scripts below and paste it to SSH terminal. Note you might need to paste text using SHIFT + INSERT. Press ENTER after scripts are pasted to terminal. Monitor terminal output. If prompted yes or no, write yes or y and press ENTER.

sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

docs.title: 8. Optional: Demo for Hosting a Website
docs.text: Here we create nginx container for hosting a simple website.

docs.title: 8.1 Create directory
docs.text:
This script creates folder called my-demo-website and enters this folder

mkdir -p ~/my-demo-website
cd ~/my-demo-website

docs.title: 8.2 Create docker-compose.yml and index.html
docs.text:
This script creates two files in folder we are in, in this case inside my-demo-website. Script creates files and then starts container.

cat > docker-compose.yml << 'EOF'
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    container_name: my-demo-website
    ports:
      - "80:80"
    volumes:
      - ./:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro
    restart: unless-stopped
EOF

cat > index.html << 'EOF'
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>Hello World</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>HELLO WORLD</h1>
</body>
</html>
EOF

docs.title: 8.2.1 Start the container
docs.text: sudo docker compose up -d

docs.title: 8.2.2 Check container status
docs.text:
sudo docker ps

Example picture how it should look like

docs.title: 8.3 Access the website
docs.text:
For accessing website we need to open port 80 in cPouta dashboard.

Go to Network → Security groups → Create security group. Name it for example ingress port 80 Add rule. We create Custom TPC rule, you can add description if you want. Add 80 in Port

Now you should be able to access your website using virtual machine floating IP. There should only be text HELLO WORD on the website.

docs.title: 9. Security
docs.text: This section explains how the documentation website and the cPouta demo environment were secured.

docs.title: 9.1 Static Site Architecture
docs.text:
The website is built with MkDocs Material and is a fully static site (HTML, CSS, JS, JSON). It does not include backend logic, databases, logins, or form handling.

Because of this:

  • SQL injection is not possible (no database)
  • XSS via search is not possible (search runs client-side and treats input as text)
  • Session, cookie, and request-forgery attacks do not apply (no authentication or state)

A static site removes many common web vulnerabilities.

docs.title: 9.2 Access Control and SSH Security
docs.text: The cPouta VM hosting the website is protected using:

docs.title: SSH key authentication
docs.text:
• Only SSH keys are allowed
  • Password login is disabled

docs.title: Security groups (firewall rules)
docs.text:
Only required ports are open:

  • 22 – SSH (restricted using CIDR)
  • 80 – HTTP (used for certificate setup)
  • 443 – HTTPS (public website)

All other inbound traffic is blocked.

docs.title: 9.3 System Hardening
docs.text:
After VM creation:

  1. System was updated: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

  2. Only necessary software was installed:

  3. Nginx (web server)
  4. Certbot (HTTPS)

  5. Docker (optional demo)

  6. No extra services were exposed.

  7. The site is served using a minimal Nginx configuration from /var/www/html/.

docs.title: 9.4 HTTPS and TLS Certificates
docs.text:
The website uses HTTPS to protect users by encrypting traffic and preventing interception.

HTTPS is enabled with Let’s Encrypt and Certbot:

   sudo certbot --nginx -d yourdomain.com

Certbot:

  • installs the TLS certificate
  • configures Nginx
  • redirects HTTP → HTTPS
  • renews certificates automatically

docs.title: 9.5 Summary
docs.text:
• Static site → eliminates many vulnerabilities
  • SSH key authentication → protects VM access
  • Security groups → only essential ports open
  • System kept updated and minimal
  • HTTPS → encrypts all traffic
  • No sensitive data is processed or stored
